# Aligning Laravel's Document Root with Your Domain

Laravel ships with a `public` directory because, by default, the web server serves files from there. This design ensures that sensitive framework files like `artisan`, `.env`, and configuration code remain inaccessible to direct HTTP requests. However, many developers prefer a clean URL structure where accessing `www.mylaravelsite.com` feels identical to visiting `www.mylaravelsite.com/public`. While this looks cleaner in the browser, simply renaming the folder or moving it to the root without adjusting server configuration leaves you exposed to critical security vulnerabilities.

The core issue isn't just about aesthetics; it is about how the web server interprets requests. If you move your application to the document root without updating the virtual host settings, the web server will serve `index.php` directly as a static file rather than executing it through PHP. More dangerously, if you rely solely on `.htaccess` rules to redirect traffic from the root to the `public` folder, you are creating a dependency that can break when caching layers or load balancers intervene.

The most robust solution involves configuring your web server to serve the `public` directory as the actual document root for your domain. This approach eliminates the need for permanent redirects and aligns the file system structure with the logical URL structure.

## Configuring Nginx

If you are using Nginx, the process is straightforward. You simply define the path to the `public` folder when setting up the server block in your configuration file.

```nginx
server {
    listen 80;
    server_name www.mylaravelsite.com mylaravelsite.com;

    root /var/www/mylaravelsite/public;
    index index.php;

    location / {
        try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string;
    }

    # ... other location blocks for assets and API
}
```

By setting `root` to the path containing the `public` folder, any request to `/` is resolved against that directory. The `$uri` variable ensures that requests for assets like `/css/style.css` resolve correctly, while the `try_files` directive handles routing to Laravel's front controller. This method avoids the overhead of an external redirect and keeps the server state consistent.

## Configuring Apache

Apache users often face this scenario when upgrading from older tutorials or shared hosting environments that default to a separate document root. While `.htaccess` rules can force a 301 redirect from `/` to `/public/`, relying on redirects for primary routing is generally discouraged in production environments due to potential performance hits and cache coherence issues.

Instead, you should modify your Apache virtual host configuration to point the `DocumentRoot` directly to the Laravel public folder.

```apache
<VirtualHost *:80>
    ServerName www.mylaravelsite.com
    DocumentRoot /var/www/mylaravelsite/public

    <Directory /var/www/mylaravelsite/public>
        AllowOverride All
        Require all granted
    </Directory>
</VirtualHost>
```

Setting the `DocumentRoot` to `/var/www/mylaravelsite/public` ensures that the web server serves files from there immediately. The `AllowOverride All` directive is crucial here; it permits `.htaccess` files within the directory to override settings, which is necessary for handling PHP routing and asset optimization rules defined in Laravel's base configuration.

## Why Not Just Use .htaccess Redirects?

You might consider keeping the root folder at `/var/www/mylaravelsite` and placing a `.htaccess` file there that redirects all requests to `/public`. While this achieves the URL appearance, it introduces a subtle complexity: the web server still sees the request as targeting the root directory. This can complicate error logging, debugging, and SSL certificate validation processes that expect the document root to match the domain exactly.

Furthermore, if you ever need to move the project or update the deployment script, maintaining a redirect layer adds an extra step of verification. Directly aligning the document root with the `public` folder removes this abstraction layer entirely.

## Security Considerations

It is vital to remember that changing the document root does not automatically secure your application. The security benefits of Laravel's `public` directory structure come from the fact that sensitive files (like `.env`, `composer.json`, and framework source code) are excluded from the web server's reachable path. By pointing the document root strictly to the `public` folder, you ensure these files remain inaccessible via HTTP requests.

If you inadvertently point the document root to the Laravel installation directory itself, a simple request to `mysite.com/config.php` or `mysite.com/.env` could leak sensitive data. Always verify that your web server configuration restricts access to non-public assets. For shared hosting environments where you cannot modify the main virtual host configuration, you may be forced to use `.htaccess` redirects as a fallback, but understanding the underlying mechanism is essential for troubleshooting.

For developers looking to deepen their understanding of Laravel's security architecture and deployment best practices, resources like https://laravelcompany.com offer further insights into securing your application beyond just server configuration.
